Remove every complete singleline Markdown link text and every bare URL beginning with , , or ., deleting the full link construct rather than retaining its label or URL. Delete every  character everywhere, including code delimiters; remove ,  and  everywhere except inside the contents of inline code spans and fenced code blocks, whose contents must otherwise remain unchanged after their backtick delimiters are removed. Remove all matches on a line, remove only the inner link in nested forms such as [text] and any resulting empty [], do not match links across line breaks, preserve all other original characters including whitespace and line breaks exactly, and output only the sanitized text with no commentary or wrapper formatting. : The strongest nonobvious approach is not to snapshot a 131,072token ExLlamaV3 cache. Snapshot only a “modelready, cacheempty” GPU process, then hide the remaining restore time behind a clientside intent signal and an edgeheld streaming request.

Architecture

1. Deploy two Modal paths: a scaletozero GPU inference function and a tiny alwaysavailable HTTP ingress/queue. The ingress accepts a request, immediately opens an SSE/WebSocket response, and holds it while the GPU function is scheduled/restored. The browser sends a signed “user is likely to submit” signal on editor focus, model selection, or after a short typing debounce; this invokes the GPU path early, but does not reserve a GPU. The first real request is therefore often served by an alreadyrestoring or restored container. At true zero, the ingress still buffers the request—the unavoidable residual latency is moved before the first token rather than exposed as a failed request. Scaletozero systems need precisely such an activator/buffer because no replica exists to receive the wakeup request Scaling GPU inference to zero and back.

2. Start speculative streaming immediately after the backend is available: emit status/commentary tokens or a deterministic short preamble while the real prompt is being prefetched and tokenized, then begin model tokens. Do not fabricate answer content. For repeated UI actions, cache the tokenized system prompt and conversation prefix, and use prefix reuse if the engine supports it. A held connection masks network and scheduling latency, but cannot make GPU restoration itself free or instantaneous.

3. Use Modal memory snapshots with GPU snapshots as an accelerator, not as the correctness boundary. Modal’s implementation restores process state and, when enabled, invokes CUDA checkpoint restoration; the GPU feature is alpha and can fall back to a nonsnapshot startup on failure Lifecycle Hooks and Memory Snapshots | modallabs/modalclient | DeepWiki. Modal reports large improvements on compatible examples—for example, a vLLM/Qwen workload from 45 seconds to 5 seconds—but these are not GLM5.3Flash/EXL3 measurements and should not be treated as a guarantee Best Open Source Models for AI Data Analysts in 2026 | Modal Blog.

ExLlamaV3/KVcache plan

• Do not construct CacheLayer_quant(max_num_tokens=131072) before the snapshot. A static 131k cache makes the snapshot include the cache’s committed/touched VRAM pages and creates a large restore and dirtypage burden even if no user has used that context.
• Initialize the model and tokenizer, load EXL3 weights, import/compile extensions, create the CUDA context, and run representative short prefill/decode probes. Then capture with a small cache policy—ideally an empty cache or a bounded serving cache such as 4k–16k tokens. Allocate a larger cache only after restore, on demand, in chunks.
• Prefer dynamic_seq_len or an explicitly lazy cache allocator if the ExLlamaV3 version exposes it. If CacheLayer_quant internally allocates the full tensor regardless of sequence length, changing the requested runtime sequence length will not solve the problem: patch the allocator so capacity grows geometrically by blocks and only new blocks are materialized. Validate that the kernel accepts noncontiguous/blockindexed KV storage; otherwise use a small static cache and accept reallocation at a controlled boundary.
• Keep K/V quantization at 8/8 only if quality requires it. Measure 4bit or the engine’s supported lowerbit format, because quantized KV is specifically valuable when longcontext cache exceeds weight memory KV Cache Implementations | huggingface/transformers | DeepWiki. A related EXL3 GLM implementation reports a 4bit KV strategy and very large context capacity, but that is a different integration and is evidence of feasibility, not proof for upstream ExLlamaV3 Architecture Overview | brandonmmusicmax/glm52exl3sparkinfer | DeepWiki.
• Never “touch” the whole cache to warm it. Avoid blanket zero/fill operations, fullcache test prompts, torch.cuda.memset across the capacity, or a 131k dummy generation before snapshot. Use nvidia-smi, torch.cuda.memory_stats(), allocator traces, and a binarysearch cache capacity benchmark to distinguish reserved from physically committed/touched memory.

A useful budget is:
KV bytes ≈ layers × tokens × KV width × (K bits + V bits)/8, plus scales, alignment, metadata, temporary workspace, and allocator fragmentation. Calculate this from GLM’s actual layer count and KV dimensions; do not infer it from parameter count. Snapshot size is likewise empirical: measure checkpoint artifact size and restore latency with cache capacities 0, 4k, 16k, 32k, and 131k.

Snapshot preparation

Before @modal.enter(snap=True) completes, warm the CUDA context, load the native EXL3 extension, execute representative GEMM/attention/prefill/decode shapes, and populate the PyTorch/FlashAttention compilation caches. Keep sockets, request objects, CUDA graph handles tied to external state, and mutable conversation state out of the snapshot. Recreate those after restore. GPU snapshots are hardware/runtimespecific rather than portable artifacts, and external connections may be invalid after restoration Lowering GPU Chilly Begins with Reminiscence Snapshots: Restoring CUDA Workloads in Seconds  Evanino.com.

The key measurement is not merely “snapshot bytes”: record (a) snapshot creation time, (b) restore/unpause time, (c) major page faults, (d) GPU memory copied/restored, (e) first CUDA call latency, and (f) firsttoken latency. A pagefaultheavy restore means the process resumed with mappings whose pages are fetched lazily; a CUDAwarmup spike means kernels/context/allocator state was not captured or was invalidated. Run one noop CUDA operation and one real prefill after restore, then compare. Do not assume CUDA graphs survive migration; treat them as an optimization to recreate if the restored graph is invalid.

Weight I/O hierarchy

1. Bake immutable EXL3 files and compiled native libraries into the image when image size and deployment cadence permit. This removes runtime networkvolume reads, and Modal describes its filesystem as optimized for fast startup Best LongContext Open Source Code LLMs for Repo Agents in 2026.
2. Otherwise store weights on a Modal Volume, but copy the active checkpoint once to local ephemeral disk/NVMe before loading. Modal Volumes persist across invocations and avoid repeated downloads Persistent Storage with Volumes | modallabs/modalexamples | DeepWiki, while the examples specifically recommend local /tmp/SSD for decompression because direct decompression into a Volume is slower network I/O Persistent Storage with Volumes | modallabs/modalexamples | DeepWiki.
3. Use memory mapping only if the loader’s access pattern and the underlying filesystem make it beneficial; mmap does not eliminate firsttouch I/O or page faults. Parallelize/shard reads and verify that the snapshot does not capture a halfpopulated mapped file.

For a multigigabyte EXL3 model, the practical sequence is Volume/image → local NVMe staging → pinned/mapped weight load → short kernel warmup → snapshot. Benchmark image layers versus VolumetoNVMe copy in the target Modal region; published NVMe figures are environmentdependent and are not Modal guarantees Best SSD for a Local LLM Model Library in 2026 | SpecPicks.

Routing tiers

Tier 0: browser intent prewarm, only for a user who has permission and has selected this model; cancel on blur/idle. Send no sensitive prompt until the actual submit.
Tier 1: CPU ingress holds the connection, tokenizes/cachehits the prompt, selects the compatible snapshot/GPU type, and starts the GPU invocation.
Tier 2: restored GPU modelready process serves normal requests.
Tier 3: if the 131k request exceeds the bounded postrestore cache, either grow it incrementally, route to a longcontext pool, or return a truthful queue/status event. Do not let rare 131k requests force every snapshot to carry 131k capacity.

Critique and correction

The tempting answer—“enable both snapshots, preallocate the full cache, and keep one worker warm”—fails the stated constraint. keep_warm=1 directly buys latency with idle GPU billing; fullcache preallocation maximizes VRAM and snapshot size; and snapshotting cannot guarantee portability or eliminate page faults. The corrected design separates immutable model state from perrequest KV state, uses predictive activation rather than standby capacity, and buffers the request at the edge. It therefore achieves zero incremental GPU standby cost, but not literally zero cost: each speculative Modal invocation that actually provisions CPU/GPU time is billable, and falsepositive prewarms waste compute. Control that with debounce, cancellation, rate limits, modelpopularity thresholds, and telemetrydriven activation. Finally, “zero TTFT” is impossible at scaletozero; the defensible goal is zero perceived TTFT for the common path and bounded, visible queueing for the cold path.

Recommended experiment: build four variants—(A) 131k static cache, (B) empty snapshot plus postrestore dynamic cache, (C) empty snapshot plus 16k static cache, and (D) no GPU snapshot—and measure p50/p95 provisioning, restore, first CUDA call, firsttoken, snapshot bytes, GPU seconds, and falsepositive prewarm rate. Select the lowestcost variant meeting the p95 TTFT target rather than assuming the largest snapshot is fastest.
